overview: Both aim to correct genetic problems, but gene therapy typically adds a working gene copy while gene editing directly changes the existing DNA sequence.
genZNote: Gene therapy: adding a spare working copy of the part that's broken. Gene editing: actually going in and fixing the broken part itself.

aspects.label: Basic Approach
aspects.valueA: Introduces a normal/functional copy of a gene into cells, usually without altering the existing faulty gene.
aspects.valueB: Directly modifies the existing DNA sequence at a precise location (e.g. using CRISPR-Cas9).

aspects.label: Precision of the Change
aspects.valueA: Adds a new gene copy; often doesn't target a specific genomic location.
aspects.valueB: Makes a precise, targeted change at a specific genomic site.

aspects.label: Example
aspects.valueA: ADA-SCID treatment using a viral vector to deliver a working ADA gene.
aspects.valueB: CRISPR-Cas9 correcting the sickle-cell mutation directly in a patient's own DNA.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: ADA-SCID (Severe Combined Immunodeficiency) is the landmark first successful human gene therapy case, frequently cited in biotechnology sections.
overlay.memoryTrick: Gene therapy = add a working copy. Gene editing = fix the actual sequence.
overlay.commonMisconception: Gene editing tools like CRISPR are not automatically classified as gene therapy — the distinction matters for how the treatment is regulated and delivered.
